journey.fortune_basis: And it was really, really interesting to me.

journey.fortune_basis: I just loved it. I loved the colleagues.
journey.quote: in the meantime, I was like doing overnights at Kaiser. And, um, I just loved it. I loved the colleagues. I loved the people there.

journey.fortune_basis: So we just went through and did a little efficiencies and things like that.
journey.quote: Jamie Goldfarb, who was an older guy, said, look, just figure out a quit complaining basically he said, and he said it more nicely, but try to find a solution.

journey.quote: I met every single person in the hospital because I had to go around and beg them to sponsor these kids, including in the OR.

journey.fortune_basis: when I interviewed with her, we just hit it off and I got that position.
journey.quote: I had been appointed it was my first big leadership position as assistant medical director under Virginia Ambrosini.

journey.fortune_basis: either way I'll be fine because I really loved what I was doing.
journey.quote: I threw my hat in the ring for that. And I, I'm sure people talked to me about it, but it was in my mind already.

journey.quote: after six years there, at the end of my term there, I would say Panorama City really turned around in terms of being excellent and having a great reputation around the region

journey.fortune_basis: people were very skeptical of me I would say, when I started.
journey.quote: In Georgia, I was brand new, nobody knew me, and some of them were resentful of Southern California coming in

journey.quote: No one on my leadership team wanted to do it. Um, no one, I maybe had two early adopters from the chief's team. Um, and yet I knew it was a good idea.

journey.year_note: Six to nine months into the Emory decision; no year given.
journey.label: Learns to bring her team along
journey.fortune_basis: it was really a lesson to me in bringing folks along.
journey.quote: I would almost all of them were 100% on board with me as a leader. I could trust them.

journey.year_note: 'Maybe even two weeks ago' in the 2026 interview.
journey.label: Still advising Georgia leaders
journey.fortune_basis: I love doing that. Very proud of that.
journey.quote: one of the leaders in Georgia who I haven't taught, you know, I haven't seen them in or haven't been there in five years. But, um, she called to ask my advice about something

events.name: Georgia region financial crisis
events.view: She described Georgia as losing money on contracted hospital and specialty care, a burning platform that made physicians ready for change.
events.quote: they needed a new hospital strategy desperately, they were part of their financial problem was hemorrhaging money into the community environment because they don't own their own hospitals there

prompt.question: What were the greatest challenges you've experienced as a leader in this organization? Greatest challenges as a leader.

events.name: Electronic health record rollout
events.view: She was there when the electronic record arrived and calls it a lasting game changer for panel care and population data.
events.quote: Kaiser's electronic health record, which came in so many years ago now was, I was there when it was first came in to the offices, was a game changer.

prompt.question: Can you discuss the impact of Kaiser Permanente's electronic health record on patient care?

events.name: COVID-19 pandemic
events.view: She credited prior video-visit certification and the Georgia team for a fast switch to virtual care, while fearing for staff safety.
events.quote: And then at some point in that spring of Covid, we flipped all our in-person appointments to video appointments, and everyone was able to do it.

prompt.question: Do you want to mention about Covid, how we were one of the first to the vaccines or.

events.name: 1990s KP financial crisis
events.view: She recalled KP nearly going bankrupt from growing too fast, and the medical group partnering with the health plan on access and patient experience.
events.quote: There was a pivotal moment, and I can't remember exactly what year it was, but I was there, when Kaiser Permanente almost went bankrupt.

prompt.question: A. Pivotal moment in the history of Kaiser Permanente that has shaped its current practice.

events.name: First women Permanente executive medical directors
events.view: She was briefly the only woman among Permanente leaders, and found the group more functional once three women served together.
events.quote: one of my claims to fame is that I was the first female president and CEO of any of the Permanente regions, and that was the Georgia region.

prompt.question: So tell me about your experience as the first female president, executive medical director of southeast, and of the program.

retellable.title: The barbecue that wasn't barbecue
retellable.summary: New to Georgia, she invited the chiefs to a rooftop 'barbecue' meaning only outdoor cooking. They expected Southern barbecue, and the mix-up became a shared laugh that helped build relationships.
retellable.quote: In California, you call anytime you cook outside a barbecue, in Georgia, barbecue means the food barbecue. Um, and so it was hilarious. They were very disappointed.
retellable.why: A warm, funny picture of a new leader building trust across cultures.

retellable.title: Allergy receptionist books a life-saving mammogram
retellable.summary: At Panorama City an allergy receptionist booked a reluctant patient's overdue mammogram during her allergy visit. The mammogram found breast cancer the patient says she would otherwise have missed.
retellable.quote: she got her mammogram booked at her allergy appointment and it was within a couple of weeks she got it. She went to her mammogram appointment and she had breast cancer.
retellable.why: Shows integrated care and proactive outreach saving a life.

retellable.title: Leading from where you stand
retellable.summary: Frustrated by wasted time getting patients roomed, the young pediatrician walked the clinic with her nurse to find delays. A senior colleague told her to stop complaining and find a solution, and she did.
retellable.quote: So we just went through and did a little efficiencies and things like that. And, um, so it's what they would later call leading from where you stand.
retellable.why: Concrete model for new physicians on turning frustration into improvement.

questions_that_opened_things_up.question: Do you want to, I think something unique is, and you mentioned it earlier, would be just to talk about what it's like to be the new kid on the block and be the leader.
questions_that_opened_things_up.why: Drew a detailed account of building trust in Georgia: rounding, home gatherings, the barbecue story.

questions_that_opened_things_up.question: something to the effect of how does a leader balance wanting to be liked with wanting to get their physicians to perform?
questions_that_opened_things_up.why: Drew her frank reflections on difficult conversations, overpromising and giving burnt-out physicians time.
